chapter.title: Callbacks, Events and Tasks
chapter.para: .NET calls back through delegates: a comparison for a sort, a predicate for a query, a handler for an event, the work of a task. A Rexx method is given to .NET as a , made by .net~handler(object, message [, options]), which becomes a delegate of whatever type .NET wants.

section.title: Handlers as Delegates
section.para: Where .NET wants a delegate (an Action, a Func, a Predicate, a Comparison, an EventHandler, any delegate type), a NetHandler becomes a delegate of that exact type. When .NET calls it, the handler's message goes to its object with the delegate's arguments, converted as any .NET value going to Rexx (a sender that Rexx already holds is the same proxy, == to it), and what the method returns goes back as the delegate's return value, converted to its type. A handler gives the same delegate each time for the same delegate type, so -= finds what += added.

A method that returns nothing where the delegate returns a value is an error, but for object (null) and Task (a completed task); so is a result that does not convert. Delegates with pointer or span parameters are not supported.

Which overload. C# chooses among overloads with delegate parameters by the lambda's parameters and body; a Rexx method declares neither. So the delegate with fewer parameters wins (Where(Func<T, bool>) before the indexed Where(Func<T, int, bool>)), then one that returns nothing before one that returns a value (Task.Run(Action) before Task.Run(Func<T>)). Another one is chosen by forcing the delegate type: .net~as(h, "System.Func<int>"). A parameter of type Delegate gets an Action. The type arguments of a generic method are not inferred from a handler: give them, or force the delegate type.

example.title: Rexx methods as delegates
example.programlisting:
h = .net~handler(.Worker~new, "WORK") t = .net~System~Threading~Tasks~Task~Run(h) -- an Action: no result t~await; say .net~typeOf(t) t = .net~System~Threading~Tasks~Task~Run(.net~as(h, "System.Func<int>")) say t~await .net~typeOf(t) l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<int>")~new do i over "5 3 8 1"~makeArray(" "); l~Add(i); end e = .net~System~Linq~Enumerable say e~ToArray(e~Where(l, .net~handler(.Worker~new, "BIG")))~makeString("L", " ") l~Sort(.net~handler(.Worker~new, "COMPARE")) say l~ToArray~makeString("L", " ")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Worker ::method work return 6 * 7 ::method big use arg x return x > 3 ::method compare use arg a, b return b - a

section.title: Which Thread Runs the Method
section.para: By default a call runs at once, on the thread .NET calls from: a sort's comparison on the Rexx thread that called Sort (nested in that call), a timer's event on a thread of .NET's pool, a window's event on its user interface thread. A thread that runs no Rexx code yet is attached to the interpreter instance for the call. Any number of threads may call at once; they take turns in the interpreter, as Rexx threads do.

A method called from another thread waits while its object is busy in a guarded method, as it would for any Rexx thread: a handler whose object may be busy (a window's object waiting in Application.Run, a loop) should be UNGUARDED. Nested on the same thread, there is no wait.

section.title: Events
section.para: An event is reached as a member: o~Click is a , and handlers are added and removed with Rexx's compound assignment, as in C#:
section.programlisting: button~Click += .net~handler(self, "CLICKED") -- add button~Click -= h -- remove: the same handler object .net~addHandler(button, "Click", h) -- add, as a call .net~removeHandler(button, "Click", h) button~add_Click(h); button~remove_Click(h) -- .NET's own accessors
section.para: The method gets the event's arguments: for the usual EventHandler pattern, sender and e. A static event is the type's: .net~Microsoft~Win32~SystemEvents~TimeChanged += h. lists an object's events. A handler can cancel what the event announces, where its arguments allow it: e~Cancel = .true.

example.title: An event handled at once, on .NET's thread
example.programlisting:
timer = .net~System~Timers~Timer~new(50) timer~AutoReset = .false t = .Ticks~new timer~Elapsed += .net~handler(t, "TICK") timer~Start call SysSleep 0.5 say t~count .net~events(timer)~makeString("L", " ")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Ticks ::attribute count ::method init expose count count = 0 ::method tick unguarded -- called on a thread of .NET's pool expose count use arg sender, e count += 1

section.title: Queued Calls and the Event Loop
section.para: With the option queued, a call does not run at once: the delegate puts it in a queue and returns, with its type's default value, and a Rexx thread takes it when it is ready. .net~nextEvent([seconds]) returns the next call, a (&nil; if none came in time), and call~dispatch sends the handler's message on that thread; .net~eventLoop does that for every call, until .net~stopEventLoop. With latest (which implies queued), a handler keeps at most one call waiting, the newest: for progress reports, where only the last one matters. This is the model of ooRexx/WASM's .js~handler, where JavaScript cannot wait for Rexx; here it is a choice, for programs that want their events on one thread, in order.
While a thread waits in nextEvent or eventLoop, it holds no interpreter lock: other Rexx threads run. A queued handler cannot answer a value nor cancel an event (it returns at once).

example.title: The event loop
example.programlisting:
loop = .Looper~new timer = .net~System~Timers~Timer~new(20) timer~Elapsed += .net~handler(loop, "TICK", "queued") timer~Start .net~eventLoop -- runs the calls here, until stopped timer~Stop say "ticks:" loop~count
::requires "net.cls" ::class Looper ::attribute count ::method init expose count count = 0 ::method tick expose count count += 1 if count = 3 then .net~stopEventLoop

section.title: Errors in Handlers
section.para: A Rexx condition in a synchronous handler becomes a RexxException in .NET (). If .NET lets it out of the call that Rexx made (directly, or wrapped, as List.Sort wraps its comparer's exceptions), the original condition is raised again in that Rexx code, with its code and message, not a 98.900 about it.

A handler called on a thread where no Rexx code waits for .NET (a timer's, the thread pool's, a thread that .NET code started) has nobody to raise it to; an exception there would end the process. So the bridge reports the condition on .error, as Rexx reports an untrapped error, with its traceback, adds a line saying that the call returned its delegate's default value, and the program goes on.

example.title: A handler's error, raised again in the caller
example.programlisting:
l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<int>")~new l~Add(2); l~Add(1) signal on syntax l~Sort(.net~handler(.Bad~new, "COMPARE")) syntax: c = condition("O") say c~code c~message
::requires "net.cls" ::class Bad ::method compare return 1 + "a"
example.screen: 41.1 Nonnumeric value ("a") used in arithmetic operation.

section.title: Command Environments (ADDRESS)
section.para: Command environments are ooRexx's own (CommandHandler, ooRexx r13288; the Open Object Rexx Reference describes it): .CommandHandler~register(name, handler) makes a handler the ADDRESS environment name of the running interpreter instance, .CommandHandler~deregister(name) removes it, and ooRexx sends each command to it as command(command, caller), caller a CommandContext. A handler written in Rexx needs no .NET. A .NET handler goes in a : .CommandHandler~register(name, .NetCommandHandler~new(handler)), handler a .NET delegate that takes the command and a Rexx.Net.RexxCommandContext, that CommandContext with its names in .NET's casing (a Func<string, RexxCommandContext, object?>, an Action<string, RexxCommandContext>, or another delegate type with those two parameters). These are the same environments that a .NET application adds with AddCommandEnvironment, with the same rules (, where RexxCommandContext's members are):

listitem.para: What the handler returns is RC (nothing: 0), whatever its sign; ERROR, FAILURE and the other conditions come from the context's RaiseError, RaiseFailure and Raise, as for a handler written in Rexx.

An error of the handler is raised in the code that sent the command: a Rexx error of Rexx code it called as itself, a .NET exception as SYNTAX 98.900, the exception in condition("O")~additional[2]. A HALT that Rexx code the handler called does not trap (ooRexx makes it SYNTAX 4.1 on the way out) is a HALT again in the code that sent the command: SIGNAL ON HALT traps it, CALL ON HALT runs, and untrapped it is SYNTAX 4.1, as a Ctrl-C would be. Any other condition that such Rexx code lets out (RAISE USER) does not reach that code yet: ooRexx 5.3.0 drops such conditions where its native API calls Rexx code (an ooRexx bug, reported).
Its output and errors go to the context's streams, which exist with ADDRESS ... WITH; without it, the handler writes to the console itself.

Handlers stack, as any registered with .CommandHandler~register: one registered for a name covers the handler in use, which register answers (&nil; if none; its command method forwards to it); deregister uncovers it, and answers the handler removed. .CommandHandler~handler(name), ~handlers(name) and ~environments show them.

A name with no handler left answers FAILURE, RC 30, as one that does not exist. A NetCommandHandler of &nil; (or of anything that is no such delegate) is SYNTAX 93.900, as ooRexx's errors for register and deregister are.

section.para: These rules are the whole family's: the ooRexx/Python, ooRexx/Lua and ooRexx/JavaScript bridges follow them too, with their host's names.

example.title: A command environment served by .NET
example.screen: rc: 49 7 x 1 = 7 / 7 x 2 = 14 / 7 x 3 = 21 98.900 System.FormatException FAILURE, rc 30

example.title: Handlers stacked, as ooRexx's CommandHandler
example.programlisting:
using System; using Rexx.Net;
Func<string, RexxCommandContext, object?> shout = (command, caller) => command.ToUpperInvariant(); using var rexx = RexxInterpreter.Create(new RexxOptions { StreamPrefixes = false }); rexx.Run(""" use arg shout .CommandHandler~register("SHOUT", .NetCommandHandler~new(shout)) -- a handler written in Rexx over it, logging and forwarding to the one covered covered = .CommandHandler~handler("SHOUT") .CommandHandler~register("SHOUT", .Logger~new(covered)) address shout "hello"; say "rc:" rc say .CommandHandler~handlers("SHOUT")~items "handlers" removed = .CommandHandler~deregister("SHOUT") -- the logger: the .NET one again say "removed:" removed~class~id address shout "again"; say "rc:" rc ::requires "net.cls" ::class Logger inherit CommandHandler ::method init expose inner use strict arg inner ::method command expose inner use arg command, caller say "log:" command return inner~command(command, caller) """, shout);
example.screen: log: hello rc: HELLO 2 handlers removed: LOGGER rc: AGAIN

section.title: How Long a Handler Lives
section.para: A handler is held while .NET can call it: by its delegates (an event that has it, a timer, a task), by the queue, by a COM event sink. When .NET no longer holds any of them, its garbage collector lets them go, and the bridge lets the handler go with them; a program that still holds the NetHandler can give it again. There is nothing to release by hand. h~release stops a handler at once, wherever .NET keeps it: its delegates do nothing from then on.

section.title: Tasks
section.para: t~await waits for a Task or a ValueTask and returns its result (). It blocks the Rexx thread, as C#'s .Result does, so it must not be used on a user interface's thread for a task that needs that thread to finish (a C# async method that continues on it, a Control.Invoke inside the task): that would never end. In an event handler of a window, let the handler return and continue in another one: task~ContinueWith(.net~handler(self, "DONE")), or with the user interface's scheduler (.net~System~Threading~Tasks~TaskScheduler~FromCurrentSynchronizationContext) when the continuation touches controls. Tasks that do not need the user interface's thread (reading a file, a web request) are fine to await from any other Rexx thread.

A Rexx method runs on .NET's thread pool through .net~System~Threading~Tasks~Task~Run(handler), which attaches the pool's thread to the interpreter for it. Its errors are reported there (), and the task completes normally.
